text: A house arrives by inheritance, too large for the two people who own it, and their answer is to bring in more people. Denmark in the 1970s, free love adopted as a household principle, shared rooms and shared meals and a crowd at the table. Anna and Erik open a marriage to a commune, and the film watches the distance between a value agreed on in the evening and the same value at breakfast, in front of witnesses. Vinterberg lets the comedy run, because the household is good company, and underneath it something colder keeps rising. The European Film Award for Best Actress came out of this, and it went where the weight sits: the arrangement does not cost everyone in the house the same. Old habits do not dissolve because a new principle has been announced. 111 minutes is long enough for that distance to open all the way.

The fear in this one is largely a matter of sound; the score took an Academy Award, and it is doing work the images decline to do. A children's author, pregnant, on holiday in Ireland, finds her hold on the real coming loose: paranoia, then hallucination, then the sight of a second version of herself. Altman works in horror without a monster here, using a house, a landscape, and 101 minutes of unreliable seeing. The Irish setting is not decoration. Emptiness is the condition that permits the doubling, since there is nobody at hand to contradict her account of an afternoon. Thriller machinery keeps the picture moving, and it does move. What it withholds is an outside witness, which leaves an audience holding a version of events that cannot be checked against anything at all.

A pair of glasses, left behind at the scene by accident, is the hinge the whole of this 1959 picture turns on. Two friends had persuaded themselves that a crime could be engineered, planned so exactly that nothing of them would remain in it, and the object that undoes the design was never part of the design. Fleischer takes his time. The early stretch belongs to the two of them and to the pleasure they take in their own cleverness, filmed without comment, which is harder to do than judgement. Crime and history are both listed here, and the second word sets the tone: this is shot as a record of something that happened rather than as an invention. The suspense is not finally about capture. It is about how long two people can keep agreeing with each other after the plan has failed them.

The trip to New York was to sit with a friend who has been diagnosed with AIDS. What happens instead happens at the edges of that visit, and Figgis will not keep the two apart: a vigil and an infidelity share a week, a city, the same raw attention to what a body is and how long it lasts. Max Carlyle directs commercials in Los Angeles and has a wife, two children, a settled life, so this is not the story of a man with nothing. It is the story of a man with everything, standing in a room where illness has made every ordinary arrangement look arbitrary. 1997, and the diagnosis here is not a metaphor for something else. Then a year passes in the cut, and the film comes back to find the thing still attached to him, no smaller than before.

The collection is missing, and the man who assembled it is dead. A New York dealer arrives in Prague expecting a transaction, porcelain examined and valued and crated and shipped, and finds that he has to reconstruct a life before he can locate its objects. Hugh Whitemore adapted Bruce Chatwin's novel, and the film keeps the posture of an inquiry: an apartment, an inventory, questions put to people who knew the late Baron Utz. It is a German production shot in English, 98 minutes, moving at the speed of a man turning a small figure under a lamp. Underneath sits the question of what it means to spend a life on things that fit in one hand, and whether that is devotion or an arrangement for staying out of everyone's reach.

The break-up went well: no scene, no accusations, an agreement that the love had simply gone. Then Anne-Marie learns that another woman has taken the place she vacated, and the composure she was proud of turns out to have been borrowed. Drama and fantasy are the listed genres, and the second is the one to attend to, because jealousy here is treated as something that enters a room and alters what can be seen in it, until an ordinary apartment begins to behave strangely. The camera stays close on one face. That performance took the César Award for Best Actress, and it has to carry a condition with no external cause and no plot prepared to justify it. What Anne-Marie wants is not Alex returned to her; it is the other woman removed from the world, and the film is exact about how little sense that makes.

Extremadura: dry country, poor country, a heat in which thinking comes apart. Pascual Duarte works land that will never be his, among people who settled long ago on what he is and see no occasion to revise it. The film gives him almost no interior, no speech that explains him, no scene of self-understanding, and assembles the conditions instead: the labour, the humiliations too small for anyone to name aloud, the long stretches with nothing in them. When violence comes it comes out of that accumulation rather than out of a flaw in the man, which is the argument being made and the reason the film is hard to put down afterwards. Ricardo Franco holds it to 94 minutes and to the plainest available camera. Spain in 1976, looking straight at its own countryside and declining to make it picturesque.

Michele stops working first, then stops going out, and the film declines to treat those as two separate events. He is a young writer carrying a guilt he cannot locate, and Vittorio De Seta films the state rather than explaining it: the sentence that will not come, the concern of other people arriving as pressure instead of help, the steady shrinking of a life to the size of the room it is lived in. Nothing has happened to him. That is the trouble, since there is no event to point at and therefore nothing anyone can offer to repair. Italy in 1966, and the register stays level where a later film would reach for crisis. What unsettles is how reasonable each small withdrawal looks at the moment it is made, and how little distance there turns out to be between all of them together.

It is filed as a comedy, and it is one, made about a country whose streets had become an open battleground. Dino Risi puts Vittorio Gassman at the centre as a rich businessman whose household has stopped working in any recognisable way, and lets him be pleasant about it, which is the cruel move: nothing in the man's manner presents itself as the problem. Italy at the end of the 1970s, permissiveness everywhere, consumer comfort installed where a shared set of values used to be, and the political killings that gave the decade the name it still carries, the Years of Lead. The comedy is in the manners. The manners hold until they do not, and the film is at its sharpest in the gap between a father who is always available and a father who is never once present.

A handbag full of valuables, found on a Roman street, and returned to its owner. Everything follows from that one decision: a bookbinder's daughter is rewarded with the job of minding a wealthy American woman's villa, and finds herself responsible for rooms she can never belong to. Monicelli made it in 1956, and the arithmetic is exact. Guido runs a petrol station and expects to marry her; Maurizio has education, manners and unlimited time. The film is light on its feet and entirely clear about what a light comedy is doing when it puts a poor girl in a rich house and hands her the telephone. Donatella's honesty is not the joke here. It is the property the plot keeps testing, to see what happens to it on contact with money.

A convict is signed out of prison to kill and signed back in when the job is done, which makes his cell the safest alibi in the country. Erik Matti runs that arrangement for 208 minutes, long enough that the machinery stops reading as a plot device and starts reading as an institution with staff, paperwork and habits. The other half belongs to Sisoy Salas, a journalist who has taken money for years and now wants an accounting for colleagues who went missing, and the film never lets him wash himself clean on the way there. The Philippines sent it out as its submission to the Academy Awards. Three and a half hours is a serious request, and it is spent on the connective tissue most crime pictures cut: the drive, the wait, the call to the office that authorises the next one.

Sixty years in an institution, entered as a young woman in the 1920s who would not behave as the decade required of her. She is released into the household of a grand-nephew she has never met, where his wife lives under a husband with cold manners and settled opinions. Peter Hall made it for television, and the format suits him: rooms, faces, conversations that stop a word short. The old woman says almost nothing at first, having had six decades of practice at withholding, and what the film follows is the younger woman starting to notice her, then starting to recognise the shape of the arrangement she is living inside herself. Britain in 1989, looking back at what was done to women who were merely inconvenient. Nobody in the story set out to be cruel, and it cost a life anyway.

A husband's life narrows as his career widens; his wife's moves the other way, and the film is built on that crossing. Eiichi is absorbed into the business of being a businessman. Naoko is left holding hours that nobody has assigned a purpose to, and Susumu Hani follows what she does with them: new acquaintances, an interest that hardens into a commitment, an attachment she had not planned for. The larger subject is quieter than the affair and harder to dramatise, which is a woman working out that she occupies a position in the world not derived from the man she married. Japan in 1963, and the patience of the thing is the method. None of it is staged as revolt. It is a person putting weight on a floor, carefully, to learn whether the floor will hold.

Seventy-seven minutes, which for this subject amounts to a position. A young woman is settled with one man and in love with another who is married, and the running time leaves no room for the apparatus such a story usually arrives with: the confrontation, the discovery, the long reckoning. What remains is duration. Waiting, arranging, the arithmetic of who is free and for how long, and the peculiar alertness a person develops when her hours are governed by somebody else's schedule and her presence in a room is conditional. Vilgot Sjöman shot it in Sweden in 1962, and the country sent it out as its submission to the Academy Awards. Small film, ordinary situation, and the camera stays with her throughout, which is itself the argument: the position is to be examined rather than settled.
